newsitem.title: CHINA: China to delay retaliation in U.S. trade dispute.
newsitem.headline: China to delay retaliation in U.S. trade dispute.

text.p: China said on Sunday it would delay by one month its plan to ban imports of some U.S. goods in retaliation for American penalties on purchases of Chinese textiles.
China had threatened to impose a temporary ban on imports of some U.S. textiles, farm goods and alcoholic drinks from December 10.

The delay was made in view of plans for further talks between the two sides and a pledge by the U.S. to review the issue, the official Xinhua news agency quoted a spokesman of the Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation as saying.
The United States slapped penalties of $19 million on Chinese textile imports in September, saying Beijing was shipping its products through third countries to avoid quota restrictions.
Beijing had said last month it would temporarily halt imports of some U.S. products if the penalties were not withdrawn.
The two sides held four days of talks in Beijing on the dispute last week. They also discussed a possible renewal of a bilateral textile accord that expires on December 31.
No agreement was reached but the two sides promised to resume discussions later this month.
Xinhua quoted the ministry spokesman as saying that the talks were a positive step.
"China always holds that trade disputes should be settled through consultations on an equal footing," the spokesman said.
"China expects to have that kind of consultation on the issues concerned and (expects to) reach an agreement with the U.S. side at an early date."
The U.S. called the talks productive but said a great deal remained to be resolved.
China's textile sales to the United States have long been a sensitive point for U.S. trade negotiators eager to reduce Washington's swelling trade deficit.

Washington said its 1995 trade deficit with China was $35 billion, making trade a major issue in ties already strained by disagreement over Taiwan, weapons sales, nuclear proliferation and copyright piracy.
